source: FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, Swine Health Management, Volume 2: Guide to Prevent and Control Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (RAP Publication 2012/27, Bangkok, 2012)
text: In breeding sows and boars, PRRS can cause loss of appetite lasting up to four days, fever, early or premature farrowing, and abortion. Death can occur in up to 10 percent or more of sows in an outbreak. Sows may develop mastitis and stop producing milk (agalactia). Some animals lose their balance or circle. In a smaller number of animals (1 to 2 percent), the ears turn reddish or blue-purple (cyanosis) — this is where the name 'blue ear disease' comes from. In the breeding herd, this acute phase typically lasts up to six weeks, with early farrowings, more stillbirths, weak piglets, and more mummified (died-in-womb) piglets. Reproductive problems can continue for 4 to 8 months before the herd returns to normal.
